claim: Movement is a key feature of animal systems.
source: Movement is a key feature of animal systems, yet its embryonic origins are not fully understood.
evidence: This is a general statement about animal biology presented in the abstract.

claim: The embryonic origins of movement are not fully understood.
source: Movement is a key feature of animal systems, yet its embryonic origins are not fully understood.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: The Drosophila miRNA miR-2b-1 plays a role in the emergence of movement.
source: using this system, discover that the Drosophila miRNA miR-2b-1 plays a role in the emergence of movement.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the behavioral pipeline developed in the study.

claim: miR-2b-1 influences the emergence of embryonic movement by exerting actions in the developing nervous system.
source: we define that miR-2b-1 influences the emergence of embryonic movement by exerting actions in the developing nervous system.
evidence: This is supported by spectral analysis, cell sorting, RNA in situs, genetic reconstitution tests, and neural optical imaging.

claim: A previously uncharacterised chloride channel encoding gene, termed Movement Modulator (Motor), is a genetic target that mechanistically links miR-2b-1 to the onset of movement.
source: we identify a previously uncharacterised (but evolutionarily conserved) chloride channel encoding gene – which we term Movement Modulator (Motor) – as a genetic target that mechanistically links miR-2b-1 to the onset of movement.
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatics, genetic manipulation of miRNA expression, and phenocopy tests.

claim: The chloride channel encoding gene Motor is evolutionarily conserved.
source: we identify a previously uncharacterised (but evolutionarily conserved) chloride channel encoding gene – which we term Movement Modulator (Motor) – as a genetic target that mechanistically links miR-2b-1 to the onset of movement.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in the manuscript.

claim: miR-2b-1 affects the emergence of movement through effects in sensory elements of the embryonic circuitry, rather than in the motor domain.
source: suggest that miR-2b-1 affects the emergence of movement through effects in sensory elements of the embryonic circuitry, rather than in the motor domain.
evidence: This is supported by cell-specific genetic reconstitution experiments, behavioral assays, and target gene analyses.

claim: This is the first miRNA system capable of regulating embryonic movement.
source: Our work thus reports the first miRNA system capable of regulating embryonic movement, suggesting that other miRNAs are likely to play a role in this key developmental process in Drosophila as well as in other species.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings based on the experimental results.

claim: Other miRNAs are likely to play a role in embryonic movement in Drosophila and other species.
source: Our work thus reports the first miRNA system capable of regulating embryonic movement, suggesting that other miRNAs are likely to play a role in this key developmental process in Drosophila as well as in other species.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the discovery of miR-2b-1's role.

claim: Movement allows animals to walk, fly, crawl, swim and maintain their posture.
source: Movement is the main output of the nervous system allowing animals to walk, fly, crawl, swim and maintain their posture, so that they can find prey, mate partners, escape predators and relocate within habitats (Biewener et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Biewener et al., 2022.

claim: Movement enables animals to find prey, mate partners, escape predators and relocate within habitats.
source: Movement is the main output of the nervous system allowing animals to walk, fly, crawl, swim and maintain their posture, so that they can find prey, mate partners, escape predators and relocate within habitats (Biewener et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Biewener et al., 2022.

claim: How developing embryos organize molecular, cellular, and physiological processes to initiate patterned movement is still unknown.
source: Despite the key biological and adaptive roles of movement across animal systems, how developing embryos manage to organise the necessary molecular, cellular, and physiological processes to initiate patterned movement is still unknown (Hassinan et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hassinan et al., 2024.

claim: How genes control the formation, maturation, and function of cellular networks underlying the emergence of motor control systems remains poorly understood.
source: Although it is clear that the genetic system plays a role, how genes control the formation, maturation, and function of the cellular networks underlying the emergence of motor control systems remains poorly understood.
evidence: This reflects the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: miRNAs are short regulatory non-coding RNAs that repress the expression of target genes.
source: Recent work in our laboratory has shown that miRNAs – which are short regulatory non-coding RNAs that repress the expression of target genes (Alonso, 2012; Bartel, 2018) – have pervasive roles in the articulation of complex movement sequences such as those involved in body posture control in the young Drosophila larva (Issa et al., 2019; Klann et al., 2021; Picao-Osorio et al., 2015; Picao-Osorio et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Alonso, 2012 and Bartel, 2018.

claim: miRNAs have pervasive roles in the articulation of complex movement sequences involved in body posture control in the young Drosophila larva.
source: Recent work in our laboratory has shown that miRNAs – which are short regulatory non-coding RNAs that repress the expression of target genes (Alonso, 2012; Bartel, 2018) – have pervasive roles in the articulation of complex movement sequences such as those involved in body posture control in the young Drosophila larva (Issa et al., 2019; Klann et al., 2021; Picao-Osorio et al., 2015; Picao-Osorio et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies from the authors' laboratory.

claim: miRNAs might be involved in the control of fundamental aspects of motor development and control.
source: these observations, as well as those from others in Drosophila and other systems (Fricke et al., 2014; Holm et al., 2022; Kadener et al., 2009; Lackinger et al., 2019; Weng et al., 2013) hinted at the possibility that miRNAs might also be involved in the control of more fundamental aspects of motor development and control.
evidence: This is an inference based on previous observations cited from multiple studies.

claim: The miRNA miR-2b-1 is necessary for normal locomotion in freshly hatched first instar larvae.
source: In this study, we first investigate the impact of miRNA regulation on Drosophila larval movement and discover that the miRNA miR-2b-1 is necessary for normal locomotion in freshly hatched first instar larvae.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from larval movement assays.

claim: The biological properties of young early larvae are defined in the embryo to a great degree.
source: Based on this finding and the fact that, to a great degree, the biological properties of young early larvae are defined in the embryo, we hypothesised that miR-2b-1 affects the emergence of movement during the embryonic stage.
evidence: This is based on established developmental biology knowledge.

claim: miR-2b-1 is essential for the normal development of embryonic movement through a role in the sensory nervous system.
source: using this new approach, we established that miR-2b-1 is indeed essential for the normal development of embryonic movement through a role in the sensory nervous system.
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral pipeline experiments and genetic analyses.

claim: Motor is a previously uncharacterised gene predicted to encode a chloride channel.
source: Through the combination of bioinformatic miRNA target prediction, gene expression and phenocopy analyses we identified a previously uncharacterised gene predicted to encode a chloride channel – which we call Motor – as a genetic link between miR-2b-1 and its effects on embryonic movement.
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic predictions and experimental validation.

claim: Motor is a genetic link between miR-2b-1 and its effects on embryonic movement.
source: Through the combination of bioinformatic miRNA target prediction, gene expression and phenocopy analyses we identified a previously uncharacterised gene predicted to encode a chloride channel – which we call Motor – as a genetic link between miR-2b-1 and its effects on embryonic movement.
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic predictions, gene expression analyses, and phenocopy tests.

claim: ΔmiR-2b-1 mutant larvae show a substantial decrease in larval speed.
source: miR-2b-1 belongs to the miR-2 family (Marco et al., 2012) and ΔmiR-2b-1 mutant larvae show a substantial decrease in larval speed (Figure 1C) suggesting that absence of this specific genetic component compromises the ability of the larva to move normally.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: miR-2b-1 belongs to the miR-2 family.
source: miR-2b-1 belongs to the miR-2 family (Marco et al., 2012) and ΔmiR-2b-1 mutant larvae show a substantial decrease in larval speed (Figure 1C) suggesting that absence of this specific genetic component compromises the ability of the larva to move normally.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Marco et al., 2012.

claim: Absence of miR-2b-1 compromises the ability of the larva to move normally.
source: miR-2b-1 belongs to the miR-2 family (Marco et al., 2012) and ΔmiR-2b-1 mutant larvae show a substantial decrease in larval speed (Figure 1C) suggesting that absence of this specific genetic component compromises the ability of the larva to move normally.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed decrease in larval speed in mutants.

claim: Early embryonic movement patterns occur during the final third of embryogenesis (14-16 hr after egg laying).
source: To monitor the onset of embryonic movement, which, in normal embryos, occurs during the final third of embryogenesis (i.e. 14–16 hr after egg laying (AEL) Crisp et al., 2008; Pereanu et al., 2007; Figure 1D and E)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Crisp et al., 2008 and Pereanu et al., 2007, and shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: A phase of disorganised movements begins around 16 hr after egg laying.
source: From this, we were able to observe distinct phases of movement that are consistent with previous data: namely, the onset of a phase of disorganised movements ~16 hr after egg laying (hAEL) and its transition into a phase characterised by rhythmic bursts of activity and inactivity ~18 hAEL (Crisp et al., 2008; Pereanu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Crisp et al., 2008 and Pereanu et al., 2007.

claim: A phase characterised by rhythmic bursts of activity and inactivity begins around 18 hr after egg laying.
source: From this, we were able to observe distinct phases of movement that are consistent with previous data: namely, the onset of a phase of disorganised movements ~16 hr after egg laying (hAEL) and its transition into a phase characterised by rhythmic bursts of activity and inactivity ~18 hAEL (Crisp et al., 2008; Pereanu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Crisp et al., 2008 and Pereanu et al., 2007.

claim: The myogenic phase of movement does not depend on neural input.
source: These phases have been termed as 'myogenic' and 'neurogenic' based on their respective dependence on neural input (Figure 1N; Crisp et al., 2008; Carreira-Rosario et al., 2021; Crisp et al., 2011; Zeng et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies and shown in Figure 1N.

claim: The neurogenic phase of movement depends on neural input.
source: These phases have been termed as 'myogenic' and 'neurogenic' based on their respective dependence on neural input (Figure 1N; Crisp et al., 2008; Carreira-Rosario et al., 2021; Crisp et al., 2011; Zeng et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies and shown in Figure 1N.

claim: Myogenic and neurogenic phases of movement have been observed in Drosophila and other systems, including vertebrates.
source: and have been observed in Drosophila, as well as in other systems, including vertebrates (Hamburger, 1963; Hamburger and Balaban, 1963; Hamburger et al., 1965; Ripley and Provine, 1972; Saint-Amant and Drapeau, 1998) strongly suggesting that this is a general feature of motor development.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies in different species.

claim: The presence of myogenic and neurogenic phases is a general feature of motor development.
source: and have been observed in Drosophila, as well as in other systems, including vertebrates (Hamburger, 1963; Hamburger and Balaban, 1963; Hamburger et al., 1965; Ripley and Provine, 1972; Saint-Amant and Drapeau, 1998) strongly suggesting that this is a general feature of motor development.
evidence: This is an inference based on observations across multiple species.

claim: Movement patterns during the early chaotic phase remain unchanged by pan-neuronal expression of Kir.
source: The results of this experiment show that whilst movement patterns during the early chaotic phase remain unchanged by this treatment (Figure 2C and E), motor activity at the rhythmic phase is almost completely eliminated (Figure 2C and F)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and E.

claim: Motor activity at the rhythmic phase is almost completely eliminated by pan-neuronal expression of Kir.
source: The results of this experiment show that whilst movement patterns during the early chaotic phase remain unchanged by this treatment (Figure 2C and E), motor activity at the rhythmic phase is almost completely eliminated (Figure 2C and F)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and F.

claim: The emergence of the rhythmic phase depends on normal neural activity.
source: The results of this experiment show that whilst movement patterns during the early chaotic phase remain unchanged by this treatment (Figure 2C and E), motor activity at the rhythmic phase is almost completely eliminated (Figure 2C and F) strongly indicating that the emergence of this latter phase depends on normal neural activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Kir expression experiment results.

claim: The movement frequencies that characterise the rhythmic phase do not emerge in Kir embryos.
source: In addition, spectral analysis demonstrates that the movement frequencies that characterise the rhythmic phase (Figure 2B and G) do not emerge in Kir embryos (Figure 2D and G).
evidence: This is supported by spectral analysis data shown in Figures 2B, D, and G.

claim: ΔmiR-2b-1 mutant embryos displayed a different pattern of embryonic movement when compared with wild type counterparts.
source: These experiments showed that ΔmiR-2b-1 mutant embryos displayed a different pattern of embryonic movement when compared with their wild type counterparts.
evidence: This is supported by the embryonic movement tracking experiments.

claim: The distinct phases of embryonic movement are clearly recognisable in ΔmiR-2b-1 mutant embryos.
source: Although the distinct phases of embryonic movement are clearly recognisable in mutant embryos, the overall amount of movement appeared greatly reduced (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is supported by observation of movement traces shown in Figure 2J.

claim: The overall amount of movement is greatly reduced in ΔmiR-2b-1 mutant embryos.
source: Although the distinct phases of embryonic movement are clearly recognisable in mutant embryos, the overall amount of movement appeared greatly reduced (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: ΔmiR-2b-1 mutant embryos show significantly lower levels of movement during the myogenic phase compared to wild type.
source: Indeed, comparison of quantity of movement in wild type and ΔmiR-2b-1 mutant embryos either during the earlier myogenic phase (Figure 2L) or during the neurogenic phase (Figure 2M) shows significantly lower levels of movement in mutants.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2L.

claim: ΔmiR-2b-1 mutant embryos show significantly lower levels of movement during the neurogenic phase compared to wild type.
source: Indeed, comparison of quantity of movement in wild type and ΔmiR-2b-1 mutant embryos either during the earlier myogenic phase (Figure 2L) or during the neurogenic phase (Figure 2M) shows significantly lower levels of movement in mutants.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2M.

claim: miRNA mutant embryos shift to a higher frequency of movement bouts during the rhythmic phase when compared to normal embryos.
source: Furthermore, spectral analyses of embryonic movement traces reveal that miRNA mutant embryos shift to a higher frequency of movement bouts during the rhythmic phase when compared to normal embryos (Figure 2I and K)
evidence: This is supported by spectral analysis data shown in Figures 2I and K.

claim: Average bout length is shortened in ΔmiR-2b-1 mutant embryos.
source: and that average bout length is also shortened (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: miR-2b-1 might exert its roles on embryonic movement, at least in part, due to action within the developing embryonic nervous system.
source: Altogether these observations suggest that miR-2b-1 might exert its roles on embryonic movement, at least in part, due to action within the developing embryonic nervous system.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed effects on the neurogenic phase.

claim: miR-2b-1 is located within the 3' untranslated region (3'UTR) of the Bruton tyrosine kinase (Btk) gene.
source: Taking advantage from the fact that miR-2b-1 is located within the 3' untranslated region (3'UTR) of the Bruton tyrosine kinase (Btk) gene (Theroux and Wadsworth, 1992; Vincent et al., 1989; Figure 3A)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Theroux and Wadsworth, 1992 and Vincent et al., 1989, and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The miR-2b-1 precursor miRNA transcript is expressed in multiple embryonic tissues, including the CNS.
source: These FISH experiments show that the miR-2b-1 precursor miRNA transcript (pre-miRNA; Bartel, 2018) is expressed in multiple embryonic tissues, including the CNS (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: miR-2b-1 is expressed in embryonic neurons.
source: To further confirm the expression of miR-2b-1 in the nervous system, we conducted fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS, Figure 3C) to isolate embryonic neuronal samples (labelled by means of elav >GFP) followed by RT-PCR for the mature miRNA transcript and observed miR-2b-1-specific signal (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by FACS and RT-PCR data shown in Figures 3C and D.

claim: elav-driven expression of miR-2b-1 in a ΔmiR-2b-1 mutant background leads to a phenotypic rescue, producing embryos that display statistically indistinguishable movement patterns to those recorded in control embryos.
source: Results in Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A show that elav-driven expression of miR-2b-1 in a ΔmiR-2b-1 mutant background leads to a phenotypic rescue, producing embryos that display statistically indistinguishable movement patterns to those recorded in control embryos
evidence: This is supported by genetic reconstitution data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Neural expression of miR-2b-1 is sufficient to restore a normal onset of embryonic movement.
source: indicating that neural expression of miR-2b-1 is sufficient to restore a normal onset of embryonic movement.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic reconstitution experiment results.

claim: When ΔmiR-2b-1 mutant larvae are developmentally provided with pan-neuronal miR-2b-1 expression, the characteristic miRNA larval mutant phenotype is rescued, with specimens moving at natural speed.
source: To further examine the biological roles of neural miR-2b-1 expression, we assessed the impact of restoring miRNA expression in embryonic neurons on first instar larval locomotor patterns using the FIM approach described above (Figure 1B and C) and observed that when ΔmiR-2b-1 mutant larvae are developmentally provided with pan-neuronal miR-2b-1 expression, the characteristic miRNA larval mutant phenotype is rescued, with specimens moving at natural speed (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by larval locomotion data shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Expression of miR-2b-1 in the nervous system is biologically relevant and sufficient to rescue the embryonic and larval movement defects observed in ΔmiR-2b-1 mutants.
source: The experiments described above strongly indicate that expression of miR-2b-1 in the nervous system is biologically relevant and sufficient to rescue the embryonic and larval movement defects observed in ΔmiR-2b-1 mutants.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic reconstitution experiments.

claim: The effects of miR-2b-1 observed at earlier stages (myogenic phase) are possibly offset by normal neural expression of miR-2b-1.
source: They also suggest that the effects of miR-2b-1 observed at earlier stages (myogenic phase) are possibly offset by normal neural expression of miR-2b-1.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the rescue experiments.

claim: No detectable morphological differences were observed in the nervous system structure between normal and ΔmiR-2b-1 mutant embryos.
source: To tease apart these potential biological effects, we examined the structure of the nervous system in normal and ΔmiR-2b-1 mutant embryos by means of immunohistochemistry and confocal microscopy and observed no detectable differences (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: miRNA mutant embryos have a reduced level of calcium dynamics when compared with their control counterparts.
source: In contrast, analysis of neural activity patterns in the embryo by means of GCaMP6 functional imaging using a movement distortion correction approach (i.e. tdTomato, Figure 3H–J; Carreira-Rosario et al., 2021), shows that miRNA mutant embryos have a reduced level of calcium dynamics when compared with their control counter parts (Figure 3K–M)
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figures 3H-M.

claim: Reduced calcium dynamics in miRNA mutant embryos occurs during a 'critical period' when neural activity levels are of crucial importance to the development of stable neural circuits.
source: notably, this occurs during a previously identified 'critical period' when neural activity levels are of crucial importance to the development of stable neural circuits (Ackerman et al., 2021; Baines and Landgraf, 2021; Giachello and Baines, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on the critical period.

claim: Artificial reduction of embryonic neural activity via optogenetic control leads to a significant decrease in larval speed.
source: Consistently with previous work, artificial reduction of embryonic neural activity via optogenetic control leads to a significant decrease in larval speed (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–G).
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–G.

claim: CG3638 is an uncharacterised Drosophila gene predicted to encode a chloride channel protein.
source: At the very top of the list was CG3638, an uncharacterised Drosophila gene predicted to encode a chloride channel protein
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic prediction using ComiR.

claim: CG3638 has broad evolutionary conservation across insects and mammals, including humans.
source: this highly ranked target was of interest to us because of its potential role in the physiological control of anionic conductances, and its broad evolutionary conservation across insects and mammals (Suzuki, 2006), including humans (Figure 4E–I).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Suzuki, 2006 and phylogenetic data shown in Figures 4E-I.

claim: Expression of CG3638 is upregulated in ΔmiR-2b-1 mutants.
source: Analysis of CG3638 expression shows that this target meets the predictions of a genuine miR-2b-1 target in full: expression of CG3638 is upregulated in ΔmiR-2b-1 mutants (Figure 4B)
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: CG3638 expression is reduced under neural over-expression of miR-2b-1.
source: and reduced under neural over-expression of miR-2b-1 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: CG3638 belongs to an evolutionarily conserved family of chloride channel genes.
source: As mentioned above, phylogenetic analysis of CG3638 reveals that it belongs to an evolutionarily conserved family of chloride channel genes (Suzuki, 2006; Suzuki and Mizuno, 2004), with representatives across distantly related lineages of insects and vertebrates including mammals, strongly indicating a functional role (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Suzuki, 2006 and Suzuki and Mizuno, 2004, and phylogenetic data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: CG3638 and its human orthologue have characteristic seven trans-membrane domains with an external carboxyterminal topology.
source: Comparison of the properties of CG3638 and its human orthologue reveal the characteristic seven trans-membrane domains with an external carboxyterminal topology (Figure 4F and H)
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figures 4F and H.

claim: AlphaFold reveals marked similarities between the proteins encoded by the Drosophila CG3638 gene and the human TTYH1 gene.
source: and applying AlphaFold – an artificial intelligence computational method able to predict protein structures with atomic accuracy (Jumper et al., 2021) – to the proteins encoded by the Drosophila CG3638 gene and the human TTYH1 gene reveals the marked similarities between these two polypeptides (Figure 4G and I).
evidence: This is supported by AlphaFold predictions shown in Figures 4G and I, and a citation to Jumper et al., 2021.

claim: A reduction in CG3638 expression in the genetic background of the miRNA mutant rescues the embryonic movement phenotype.
source: The results of this experiment show that this is indeed the case, with embryonic movement of the ΔmiR-2b-1 mutant effectively rescued by a reduction in CG3638 (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is supported by embryonic movement data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: Restoring expression of miR-2b-1 in the motor neuronal domain defined by the OK371 driver is insufficient to affect the defective movement patterns observed in miR-2b-1 null mutants.
source: Here we observe that restoring expression of miR-2b-1 in the motor neuronal domain defined by the OK371 driver is insufficient to affect the defective movement patterns observed in miR-2b-1 null mutants (Figure 1B and C and Figure 4M, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by genetic reconstitution data shown in Figure 4M and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Re-establishing expression of miR-2b-1 in all eight chordotonal organs leads to a full rescue of the motor phenotype.
source: In contrast, re-establishing expression of the miRNA in all eight chordotonal organs leads to a full rescue of the motor phenotype (Figure 4N, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is supported by genetic reconstitution data shown in Figure 4N and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The chordotonal system might be where miR-2b-1 exerts relevant actions during the normal development of movement.
source: suggesting that this aspect of the sensory system might be the one where miR-2b-1 exerts relevant actions during the normal development of movement.
evidence: This is an inference based on the chordotonal-specific rescue experiment.

claim: The mature miR-2b-1 transcript is expressed in FACS-isolated embryonic chordotonal organs prepared from wild type embryos.
source: In line with this, we observe that the mature miR-2b-1 transcript is indeed expressed in FACS-isolated embryonic chordotonal organs prepared from wild type embryos (Figure 4P)
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 4P.

claim: Motor is expressed in chordotonal organs in normal embryos.
source: and, that the genetic target of miR-2b-1, Motor, is also expressed in these cells in normal embryos (Figure 4Q, top).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4Q.

claim: Expression of Motor in chordotonal organs prepared from miR-2b-1 null mutants is up-regulated.
source: In addition, expression of Motor in chordotonal organs prepared from miR-2b-1 null mutants is up-regulated (Figure 4Q, bottom)
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4Q.

claim: Artificial reduction of Motor specifically within the chordotonal system is sufficient to rescue normal movement patterns.
source: Furthermore, artificial reduction of Motor implemented as a stratagem to decrease the effects of de-repression specifically within the chordotonal system is sufficient to rescue normal movement patterns (Figure 4R).
evidence: This is supported by larval movement data shown in Figure 4R.

claim: miR-2b-1 impacts the emergence of embryonic movement, at least in part, via effects on the sensory circuit components that underlie motor development, rather than affecting the actual generation of motor patterns.
source: Altogether, these findings strongly suggest that miR-2b-1 impacts the emergence of embryonic movement, at least in part, via effects on the sensory circuit components that underlie motor development, rather than affecting the actual generation of motor patterns.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cell-specific reconstitution experiments.

claim: The embryonic pipeline may be suitable for testing the effects of drugs and compounds on early motor activity.
source: It has not escaped our attention that our platform may be suitable for testing the effects of drugs and compounds on early motor activity and are indeed exploring this possibility.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications of the platform.

claim: Understanding the molecular elements controlling the onset of motor development in Drosophila will help understand the molecular basis of embryonic movement in other species, including vertebrates.
source: Understanding the molecular elements controlling the onset of motor development in Drosophila will put us one step closer to understanding the molecular basis of embryonic movement in other species, including vertebrates, whose embryos seem to undergo remarkably similar transition phases to those reported here (Hamburger, 1963).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the conservation of movement phases across species, supported by a citation to Hamburger, 1963.

claim: Vertebrate embryos undergo remarkably similar transition phases to those reported in Drosophila.
source: Understanding the molecular elements controlling the onset of motor development in Drosophila will put us one step closer to understanding the molecular basis of embryonic movement in other species, including vertebrates, whose embryos seem to undergo remarkably similar transition phases to those reported here (Hamburger, 1963).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hamburger, 1963.

claim: The L1 larva is a convenient model to investigate the genetics of movement.
source: The L1 larva is a convenient model to investigate the genetics of movement given that: (i) the assembly of the machinery for movement must be fully completed by this developmental stage so as to satisfactorily propel the animal into the external world, and (ii) if analysed sufficiently early, for example during the first few minutes after hatching, the animal had no real chance of compensating or learning ways around a putative defect, increasing the probability of detecting a movement phenotype by means of a suitable motor test.
evidence: This is based on reasoning about the developmental stage and timing of analysis.

claim: The assembly of the machinery for movement must be fully completed by the L1 larval stage.
source: The L1 larva is a convenient model to investigate the genetics of movement given that: (i) the assembly of the machinery for movement must be fully completed by this developmental stage so as to satisfactorily propel the animal into the external world
evidence: This is based on developmental biology knowledge.

claim: If analysed sufficiently early after hatching, the L1 larva had no real chance of compensating or learning ways around a putative defect.
source: and (ii) if analysed sufficiently early, for example during the first few minutes after hatching, the animal had no real chance of compensating or learning ways around a putative defect, increasing the probability of detecting a movement phenotype by means of a suitable motor test.
evidence: This is based on reasoning about the timing of analysis and developmental plasticity.

claim: A single miRNA, miR-2b-1, had a significant impact on larval movement.
source: To extract a signature of larval movement, we applied a whole animal imaging method based on frustrated total internal reflection (FTIR; Risse et al., 2017; Risse et al., 2013) which renders high resolution and high contrast movies to both normal and miRNA mutant first instar larvae. This led us to discover that a single miRNA, miR-2b-1, had a significant impact on larval movement (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by FTIR imaging data shown in Figures 1B and C.

claim: Previous work provided an excellent first characterisation of the onset of embryonic movement patterns in wild type embryos.
source: Previous work had provided an excellent first characterisation of the onset of embryonic movement patterns in wild type embryos (Crisp et al., 2008; Pereanu et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Crisp et al., 2008 and Pereanu et al., 2007.

claim: Early studies on embryonic movement were based on manual annotation of videotaped muscle contractions or GFP-labelled muscle Z-lines analysed under spinning disc confocal microscopy.
source: these early studies were based on the manual annotation of representative videotaped muscle contractions (Pereanu et al., 2007) or GFP-labelled muscle Z-lines analysed under spinning disc confocal microscopy (Crisp et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pereanu et al., 2007 and Crisp et al., 2008.

claim: Previous approaches to studying embryonic movement were highly labour intensive and lacked the necessary throughput required to simultaneously analyse large numbers of embryos.
source: Despite their attributes, these approaches were highly labour intensive and lacked the necessary throughput required to simultaneously analyse large numbers of embryos enabling a sensitive genetic screen.
evidence: This is a characterization of previous methods based on their limitations.

claim: Even a subtle movement performed by the embryo results in a change in the path of reflected light, leading to variations in signal intensity detected by individual pixels in the CCD sensor.
source: The camera captures the reflected light after its physical contact with the embryo; in this setting, even a subtle movement performed by the embryo results in a change in the path of reflected light, leading to variations in signal intensity detected by individual pixels in the CCD sensor, allowing for an accurate measurement of embryonic movement (Figure 1I and J).
evidence: This describes the physical principle underlying the imaging method, illustrated in Figures 1I and J.

claim: The imaging approach allows for an accurate measurement of embryonic movement.
source: The camera captures the reflected light after its physical contact with the embryo; in this setting, even a subtle movement performed by the embryo results in a change in the path of reflected light, leading to variations in signal intensity detected by individual pixels in the CCD sensor, allowing for an accurate measurement of embryonic movement (Figure 1I and J).
evidence: This is based on the physical principle of the method and validation through experiments.

claim: ComiR integrates multiple miRNA target prediction algorithms seeking to identify a set of consistent bona fide miRNA targets.
source: In this regard, ComiR integrates multiple miRNA target prediction algorithms – each one with its intrinsic strengths and weaknesses (Betel et al., 2010; Kertesz et al., 2007; McGeary et al., 2019; Miranda et al., 2006) – seeking to identify a set of consistent bona fide miRNA targets that satisfy the filters of multiple algorithms, thus reducing the generation of false positives (Bertolazzi et al., 2020; Coronnello and Benos, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations describing the ComiR method.

evidence: This is supported by citations to Bertolazzi et al., 2020 and Coronnello and Benos, 2013.

source: A genuine genetic target for a given miRNA is predicted to: (i) be de-repressed (up-regulated) in the absence of the miRNA; and (ii) be down-regulated under miRNA ectopic expression.
evidence: This is based on established principles of miRNA regulation.
